options: Banks must hold a share of short-term CHF liabilities in liquid assets on average over a maintenance period
Reserves must be met exactly on every single day
They apply only to foreign banks
Switzerland has no minimum reserve requirement
questions.explanation: Averaging over the maintenance period lets banks absorb daily liquidity swings — an important buffer mechanism for day-to-day repo activity.

questions.question: What role does intraday liquidity play in a bank's repo operations?
options: It bridges timing gaps between incoming and outgoing payments in an RTGS system and is typically sourced against collateral from the central bank
It is irrelevant because all payments net at end of day
It is sourced exclusively unsecured in the interbank market
It only concerns foreign exchange trading
questions.explanation: In an RTGS system every payment must be individually covered. Intraday facilities against collateral prevent payment gridlock, which makes managing the collateral buffer through the day operationally critical.

questions.question: Which is the SNB's main instrument for signalling its monetary policy stance today?
options: The SNB policy rate, to which it aligns short-term secured money market rates
A fixed target band for the money supply M3
A fixed exchange rate parity against the euro
Direct lending to corporates
questions.explanation: Since 2019 the SNB has communicated the SNB policy rate and seeks to keep short-term secured money market rates, especially SARON, close to it.

questions.question: What is the SNB policy rate?
options: The rate with which the SNB communicates its monetary policy stance and to which it steers short-term secured money market rates
The rate at which the SNB lends to the Swiss Confederation
The average rate of all repo trades on CO:RE
The maximum rate banks may charge on mortgages
questions.explanation: The policy rate is a signal plus a steering target. The SNB aims to keep secured money market rates, SARON above all, close to it — which is why the repo market is the transmission channel for Swiss monetary policy.

questions.question: How does a central bank inject liquidity via repo operations?
options: It buys securities under a repo and credits banks with central bank money (liquidity-providing)
It sells foreign currency reserves against francs
It permanently reduces minimum reserve requirements to zero
It issues shares in the capital market
questions.explanation: Liquidity-providing repos increase banks' sight deposits. Conversely, reverse repos or issuing the central bank's own debt instruments absorb liquidity.

questions.question: What is the purpose of SNB Bills?
options: To absorb liquidity from the banking system
To finance the federal budget
To recapitalise the SNB
To provide foreign currency liquidity
questions.explanation: SNB Bills are short-term, usually discounted debt obligations issued by the SNB. Banks exchange sight deposits for bills, which binds central bank money — and the bills themselves are eligible collateral.

questions.question: Between which hours does the SNB make intraday liquidity available by posting quotes on CO:RE?
options: Only between 12:00 and 13:00 CET
questions.explanation: The SNB posts quotes in the IN and TIN contract types across the trading day, so participants can source intraday liquidity whenever payment flows require it.

questions.question: What are 'SNB eligible securities'?
options: Securities meeting the SNB's admission criteria and accepted as collateral in its monetary policy operations
All securities listed on the SIX Swiss Exchange
Only bonds of the Swiss Confederation
Securities held in the SNB's own portfolio
questions.explanation: The SNB defines criteria on credit quality, currency, issuer, minimum size and tradability. Eligibility increases a security's liquidity and hence its value in the market.

questions.question: How does the SNB conduct its regular auctions of short-term paper on the SIX infrastructure?
options: Through the primary auction segment of the OTC spot market, at regular intervals and fixed times
Through bilateral phone trades only
Through the equity market of SIX Swiss Exchange
Through an external auction platform in Frankfurt
questions.explanation: The primary market segment exists for issuing new securities or increasing existing ones; bilateral trading outside auctions is not possible there. The auctioneer must be set up as security owner and enabled by SIX Repo AG.

questions.question: What margin ratio applies to the SNB's intraday (IN) and tomorrow-intraday (TIN) contract types on CO:RE?
options: 1.1, i.e. 110% collateral relative to cash
questions.explanation: The SNB requires 110% coverage on its liquidity-providing contract types, noticeably more conservative than the 100% margin ratio on standard interbank bond GC.

questions.question: What is the SNB's liquidity shortage financing facility (LSFF)?
options: A standing facility letting banks bridge unexpected liquidity shortfalls against SNB eligible collateral at a special rate
A fund to rescue insolvent banks
A programme to purchase corporate bonds
A facility for unsecured emergency loans without collateral
questions.explanation: The LSFF is a secured standing facility priced at a premium over the policy rate so it stays a fallback rather than a funding source. It is not emergency liquidity assistance for a failing institution.

questions.question: When does the SNB hold its special-rate LSFF repo auction on CO:RE?
options: From 18:00 to 18:15 CET on business days
At 07:00 CET before trading opens
At 12:00 CET each day
Only on the last business day of a month
questions.explanation: The auction sits at the very end of the business day, after regular trading, so banks can cover a shortfall identified once the day's payment flows are known. The contract type is CHF ON against the SNB GC basket with a 1.1 margin ratio.

questions.question: Why are standing facilities usually priced above prevailing market rates?
options: So they act as a backstop of last resort rather than a routine funding source, keeping activity in the interbank market
To generate profit for the central bank
Because they carry no collateral requirement
Because they have longer maturities than market funding
questions.explanation: A penalty spread preserves the incentive to trade with peers first. If the facility were cheap, the interbank market would hollow out and the central bank would intermediate everything.

questions.question: What does leverage mean for a bank's balance sheet?
options: Funding assets with borrowed money, so total assets are large relative to equity
Holding assets in more than one currency
Taking directional positions in interest rates
Lending to counterparties with low credit ratings
questions.explanation: Repo is a leverage machine: a bond can be bought and repoed out to fund most of its price, and the proceeds used again. The Basel leverage ratio caps this by measuring exposure without risk weights, which is why repo books consume balance sheet even when they carry little risk.

questions.question: How does a short-dated repo (residual maturity under 30 days) generally affect the liquidity coverage ratio?
options: It creates an outflow within the 30-day window whose weight depends on the quality of the collateral posted
It has no effect on the LCR at all
It always improves the LCR regardless of collateral
It is only relevant for the leverage ratio
questions.explanation: Funding secured by Level 1 HQLA is treated as largely stable in the LCR, funding against lower quality collateral much less so. That makes maturity and collateral quality active steering levers in a repo book.

questions.question: What does the net stable funding ratio (NSFR) measure?
options: Whether long-term assets are backed by sufficiently stable funding over a one-year horizon
Whether enough liquid assets exist for 30 days of stress
The ratio of capital to risk-weighted assets
The maximum leverage of a bank
questions.explanation: The NSFR structurally penalises funding long assets with very short repos and was a major driver of the lengthening of repo maturities after the financial crisis.

questions.question: Why is the leverage ratio particularly relevant for repo desks?
options: Repos lengthen the balance sheet and netting is only permitted under narrow conditions
Repos are entirely off balance sheet
The leverage ratio only captures derivatives
Repos are risk-weighted at 0%
questions.explanation: Because the leverage ratio is unweighted, a matched book consumes balance sheet even when it carries little risk. This explains window dressing around quarter ends.

questions.question: What capital benefit does clearing a repo through a CCP offer?
options: Multilateral netting and the low risk weight for qualifying CCPs reduce risk-weighted assets
All capital requirements disappear
The haircut may be set to zero
The trades no longer need to be reported
questions.explanation: Exposures to qualifying CCPs carry very low risk weights, and multilateral netting shortens the balance sheet further. Default fund contributions do, however, also attract capital.

questions.question: Why do banks sometimes reduce repo volumes shortly before quarter end?
options: Because leverage ratio and other metrics are reported on point-in-time balance sheet figures at period end
Because the repo market closes at quarter end
Because central banks prohibit repos at quarter end
Because settlement cycles lengthen at quarter end
questions.explanation: Point-in-time reporting rewards balance sheet shrinkage on the reporting date, which historically caused visible year-end and quarter-end distortions in repo rates and volumes.

questions.question: What does the CSDR settlement discipline regime cover?
options: Measures against settlement failures, in particular cash penalties for late delivery
Authorisation of trading venues
Reporting of repo trades to trade repositories
Calculation of haircuts
questions.explanation: Daily penalties are meant to improve settlement discipline. Because a repo has two settlement legs, repo books are doubly exposed to it.

questions.question: Which change to the settlement cycle is planned for the EU, Switzerland and the UK on 11 October 2027?
options: The move from T+2 to T+1 for securities transactions
The move from T+1 to T+0
The move from T+3 to T+2
The abolition of fixed settlement cycles
questions.explanation: The US moved to T+1 in 2024 and the European migration is coordinated for 11 October 2027. SIX has already published OTC spot market specifications reflecting the change; for repo desks it compresses collateral and fails management timelines.

questions.question: What is the GMRA?
options: The internationally used master agreement for repo transactions, published by ICMA
A reporting standard for securities financing transactions
A Basel III metric
The master agreement for OTC derivatives
questions.explanation: The Global Master Repurchase Agreement governs margining, substitution, events of default and close-out netting. For derivatives the equivalent is the ISDA Master Agreement.

questions.question: What does the Swiss Financial Market Infrastructure Act (FinfraG/FMIA) govern, among other things?
options: Authorisation and obligations of financial market infrastructures such as trading venues, CSDs and central counterparties
Taxation of securities transactions
Minimum reserve requirements for banks
Accounting rules for insurers
questions.explanation: FinfraG is the regulatory framework for Swiss market infrastructure. FINMA supervises, with the SNB additionally overseeing systemically important infrastructures.

questions.question: Which document set governs the relationship between a participant and SIX Repo AG?
options: The SIX Repo Rule Book together with the product specifications and the price list
The GMRA alone
The FinfraG alone
The participant's internal trading policy
questions.explanation: Participation, termination and conduct on the platform follow the Rule Book; the product specifications define tradeable contract types and the price list the fee regime. The GMRA-style master agreement sits alongside, governing the trades themselves.

questions.question: Why do legal opinions on close-out netting matter in repo business?
options: They confirm netting is enforceable in the relevant jurisdiction, which is a precondition for regulatory netting recognition
They replace the master agreement
They are only needed for derivatives
They determine the applicable haircut
questions.explanation: Without enforceable netting, exposures must be capitalised gross. ICMA commissions annual netting opinions for many jurisdictions, and their coverage effectively determines with whom a bank may net.

questions.question: What is the practical consequence of using a master agreement rather than individual contracts per trade?
options: All trades form a single legal relationship, so they can be closed out and netted to one amount on default
Each trade can be enforced separately in court
Reporting obligations fall away
Collateral no longer needs valuing
questions.explanation: The single-agreement concept is the legal foundation of netting. Without it, an insolvency administrator could cherry-pick profitable trades and disclaim the rest.

questions.question: What does an LEI identify?
options: A legal entity in financial market reporting
An individual security
A trading system
An individual transaction
questions.explanation: The Legal Entity Identifier (20 characters) identifies counterparties. Securities are identified by ISIN and transactions by UTI.

questions.question: What does SFTR (Securities Financing Transactions Regulation) govern?
options: Reporting of securities financing transactions to trade repositories plus transparency and re-use requirements
Capital requirements for trading books
Authorisation of trading venues in Switzerland
Settlement periods in securities trading
questions.explanation: SFTR grew out of the G20 work on shadow banking. It creates transparency over repos, securities lending, buy/sell-backs and margin lending.

questions.question: By when must an SFTR-reportable transaction be reported?
options: By the working day following conclusion of the trade (T+1)
Within 15 minutes of execution
By the end of the calendar week
Within 30 days
questions.explanation: Both counterparties report to a registered trade repository by T+1, and modifications and terminations are reportable too.

questions.question: What is a UTI in a reporting context?
options: A unique trade identifier reported identically by both counterparties so their reports can be matched
An internal client key of the bank
The ISIN of the delivered collateral
An identifier for the triparty agent
questions.explanation: Without a shared UTI the trade repository cannot pair the two reports of the same trade, which is why UTI generation and exchange logic is agreed contractually.

questions.question: What kind of data must be reported under SFTR?
options: Counterparties, trade terms, collateral details, haircuts, margin data and re-use information
Only the nominal amount
Only the names of the traders
Only the details of the master agreement
questions.explanation: The reporting scope is very granular — roughly 155 fields across several tables — which makes data quality and reconciliation a continuous operational challenge.

questions.question: Can a counterparty delegate its SFTR reporting to someone else?
options: Yes, reporting can be delegated, but legal responsibility for completeness and accuracy stays with the counterparty
No, reporting must always be done in-house
Yes, and responsibility transfers to the delegate as well
Only if the counterparty trades below a volume threshold
questions.explanation: Delegation to a broker, agent or vendor is common practice and does not transfer liability. It is one of the main reasons firms reconcile their delegated reports against their own books.

questions.question: Which identifiers answer 'which legal entity', 'which security' and 'which transaction' respectively?
options: LEI, ISIN and UTI
ISIN, LEI and UTI
UTI, ISIN and LEI
LEI, UTI and ISIN
questions.explanation: Keeping the three apart is fundamental to any reporting stack: the LEI identifies the counterparty, the ISIN the instrument, and the UTI the individual trade — the last of which both parties must report identically for the reports to match.

questions.question: Which transactions fall within the SFTR definition of securities financing transactions?
options: Repos, reverse repos, securities and commodities lending and borrowing, buy/sell-backs and margin lending
Only classic repos
Only interest rate derivatives
Only transactions with central banks
questions.explanation: The scope deliberately captures economically equivalent structures, so a firm cannot escape reporting by dressing a repo as a buy/sell-back.

questions.question: Which risk remains against the counterparty even in a fully collateralised repo?
options: The risk that liquidation proceeds of the collateral fall short of the claim after a default
No counterparty risk remains at all
Only currency risk
Only operational risk
questions.explanation: Collateral greatly reduces credit risk but does not eliminate it: gap risk remains — market losses between default and liquidation may exceed the haircut.

questions.question: What is wrong-way risk?
options: Exposure to a counterparty rises precisely when that counterparty's creditworthiness deteriorates
The risk of booking a trade in the wrong direction
The risk that rates move against expectations
The risk of an incorrect delivery instruction
questions.explanation: Example: collateral issued by an entity in the same region or sector as the counterparty. This is why every basket excludes closely related issuers.

questions.question: What risk does the cash lender run if the collateral is illiquid?
options: Liquidation risk: in a default the collateral can only be sold at a significant discount or with delay
No risk at all, since it owns the collateral
Only currency risk
Only operational risk
questions.explanation: This is why the haircut and the margin period of risk are calibrated to the expected liquidation horizon of the paper.

questions.question: What does the margin period of risk (MPoR) describe?
options: The period from the last successful margin exchange until the position is fully closed out after a default
The deadline for answering a margin call
The maturity of the repo
The interval between two collateral valuations
questions.explanation: The longer the MPoR, the larger the potential market move and the higher the necessary haircut. It is the central parameter in the regulatory exposure calculation for secured transactions.

questions.question: How does the haircut interact with the margin ratio when assessing a trade's risk protection?
options: They express the same protection differently — a margin ratio above 100% and a positive haircut both mean the collateral value exceeds the cash amount
They are independent and must both be applied
A margin ratio always overrides a haircut
A haircut applies to cash and a margin ratio to securities
questions.explanation: Platforms and agreements differ in which convention they use — SIX Repo product specifications quote a margin ratio, the GMRA world often speaks of haircut or initial margin — but the economics are the same.

questions.question: What happens on an event of default under the GMRA?
options: All outstanding transactions are accelerated, valued and set off against each other into one net amount
Each transaction is litigated separately
Transactions continue unchanged to their original maturity
The triparty agent assumes the defaulting party's obligations
questions.explanation: Close-out netting is the central risk mitigant: acceleration, valuation at market and set-off to a single net balance — provided it is enforceable in the relevant jurisdiction.

questions.question: What function does a central counterparty (CCP) perform in repo?
options: It interposes itself by novation, becoming buyer to every seller and seller to every buyer
It merely administers the collateral for both sides
It runs the trading platform
It reports the trades to the supervisor
questions.explanation: Through novation the CCP replaces bilateral credit risk with exposure to the CCP, backed by initial margin, variation margin and a default fund.

questions.question: What layers does a CCP default waterfall typically use?
options: The defaulter's margin, its default fund contribution, the CCP's own capital (skin in the game), then surviving members' contributions
Only state guarantees
Only the defaulter's initial margin
Only insurance policies
questions.explanation: The waterfall follows a 'defaulter pays' logic: the party causing the loss is exhausted first before mutualised resources are touched.

questions.question: What does a triparty agent NOT do in a counterparty default?
options: Assume the defaulting party's obligations or guarantee performance
Value the collateral
Report the collateral positions
Support the collateral release process
questions.explanation: The triparty agent is an operational service provider. If a counterparty defaults, the surviving party enforces its rights under the master agreement — the agent does not step into the trade.

questions.question: Which are typical lifecycle events of a live repo?
options: Substitution, repricing, margin transfer, partial return, rollover and early termination
Only the repurchase at maturity
Only a change of counterparty
Only coupon payments
questions.explanation: A repo system must represent all of these cleanly, including their effect on reporting (SFTR modifications) and on the accounting records.

questions.question: What is a rollover in repo?
options: A maturing trade is replaced at maturity by a new, often identically structured trade
Transfer of a trade to another counterparty
An increase of the haircut during the trade
A switch from bilateral to cleared
questions.explanation: Dependence on continual rollovers is a classic liquidity risk: if the market refuses to roll in stress, funding needs crystallise abruptly.

questions.question: What is a settlement fail?
options: A transaction is not delivered or not paid on the agreed settlement date
A trade is executed at the wrong price
The counterparty defaults
A margin call is calculated too late
questions.explanation: Fails cause penalties, tie up liquidity and propagate through onward delivery chains. In repo, a fail on the far leg is particularly awkward because the cash borrower does not get its collateral back.

questions.question: Why is funding long-dated, illiquid assets with overnight repos considered risky?
options: Because of maturity transformation: funding must be renewed daily while the asset stays committed long term
Because overnight repos are more expensive than term repos
Because overnight repos are prohibited by regulation
Because no collateral can be posted for them
questions.explanation: Exactly this pattern produced runs on repo-funded balance sheets in 2007/08. The NSFR addresses it directly by requiring stable funding for long-term assets.

questions.question: What is the risk profile of an open repo compared with a fixed-term repo?
options: It carries rollover and liquidity risk similar to overnight funding because either side can terminate on demand
It carries less liquidity risk because it has no fixed maturity
It carries no market risk on the collateral
It carries higher settlement risk because it never matures
questions.explanation: Open trades save daily rollover effort but should be treated as overnight money for liquidity purposes: the funding can disappear on any day the counterparty chooses.

questions.question: Which operational control is especially important in repo operations?
options: Daily reconciliation of positions, collateral holdings and margin calculations with counterparties and the triparty agent
Monthly review of trading limits
Annual review of ISIN static data
Quarterly checking of interest calculations
questions.explanation: Differences in valuation, haircut or accrued interest lead to margin disputes. Daily reconciliation is what allows them to be spotted and resolved early.

questions.question: What is a margin dispute and how is it usually resolved?
options: A disagreement about the exposure or collateral value, resolved by reconciling valuations, haircuts and accrued interest and settling the undisputed amount
A dispute about the trade date, resolved by the CCP
A dispute about the repo rate, resolved by the platform
A dispute about the master agreement, resolved by ICMA
questions.explanation: Standard practice is to transfer the undisputed portion promptly and work the difference separately, so operational disagreement does not become uncollateralised exposure.

questions.question: Why does the shaping of large repo transactions into tranches reduce risk?
options: A single failing tranche blocks a smaller amount instead of the entire transaction
It reduces the counterparty's credit risk
It lowers the transaction fee
It removes the need for a haircut
questions.explanation: Shaping supports all-or-nothing settlement per tranche and limits the economic impact of settlement failures, which matters when single trades reach nine-figure sizes.

questions.question: Why do cut-off times represent an operational risk in a multi-currency repo book?
options: Because each currency closes for settlement at a different time, so a late trade or late collateral movement can fail to settle that day
Because they determine the repo rate
Because they set the haircut
Because they define the margin ratio
questions.explanation: CZK cuts off at 11:45 while USD runs to 17:55, so a book spanning both must sequence funding decisions to the earliest deadline, not the latest.

questions.question: What is general collateral (GC)?
options: A contract type where the collateral is a basket of broadly interchangeable securities, so the trade is cash-driven
A single security that is in high demand
Collateral pledged to a central bank only
Collateral that carries no haircut
questions.explanation: In GC the cash lender is largely indifferent to which paper it receives out of the basket. Pricing therefore reflects the cost of money, not the scarcity of a bond.

questions.question: What is a 'special' in repo?
options: A security in high demand that trades at a repo rate below the GC rate
A trade with an unusually long maturity
A repo with a central bank
A basket containing only government bonds
questions.explanation: On CO:RE, specials are traded as SPC contract types where the collateral is a single security rather than a basket, with a variable term and a fixed repo rate.

questions.question: When would a trader choose an SPC contract type rather than a GC contract type?
options: When the objective is to obtain or lend one specific security rather than to move cash
When the trade size is very large
When the term is longer than one month
When the counterparty is the central bank
questions.explanation: GC serves cash-driven business; SPC serves securities-driven business. On CO:RE, SPC types are variable term with a fixed repo rate and the collateral is a named security.

questions.question: How does a squeeze in a special arise?
options: Demand for a specific security exceeds available supply, pushing its repo rate well below GC and potentially negative
The price of the security falls below par
The central bank raises the policy rate
The haircut on the security is set to zero
questions.explanation: Triggers are large short positions, small issue sizes or paper locked up in central bank holdings. Whoever owns the security can fund itself extremely cheaply.

questions.question: What is securities lending?
options: The temporary transfer of securities against collateral, remunerated by a lending fee, with an obligation to return equivalent securities
The outright sale of securities with no obligation to return them
A loan of cash secured by securities and priced as an interest rate
The pledging of securities to a central bank
questions.explanation: Repo and securities lending are economically close and both are SFTs under SFTR. The visible differences are the pricing convention — a fee rather than an interest rate — and that collateral may be cash or securities.

questions.question: What is a sell/buy-back?
options: A spot sale of securities combined with a separate agreement to buy them back forward at an agreed price
A repo in which the collateral is sold to a third party
The sale of a security followed by an option to repurchase it
A purchase of securities financed with a bank loan
questions.explanation: Economically it does the same job as a repo. The structural difference is that it is built as two formally separate trades rather than one contract with two legs.

questions.question: What distinguishes securities lending from a classic repo?
options: Securities lending is securities-driven and remunerated by a lending fee; collateral may be cash or securities
Securities lending is unsecured
Securities lending involves no transfer of title
Securities lending is only permitted between central banks
questions.explanation: Economically the two are close cousins and both are SFTs under SFTR; they differ in how they are priced (fee versus rate) and in motivation.

questions.question: What is an open repo?
options: A repo with no fixed maturity that either side can terminate on demand, with the rate periodically reset
A repo with no collateral
A repo that is publicly tendered
A repo with a variable cash amount
questions.explanation: On CO:RE, OPEN contract types have an open repurchase date type, are terminable on demand and typically carry a variable rate.

questions.question: What is a term repo?
options: A repo with a fixed agreed maturity and repurchase date
A repo transacted only with the central bank
A repo with a floating rate
A repo with no haircut
questions.explanation: Term repos — typically one week to twelve months — provide funding certainty and are more favourable for NSFR and liquidity buffers than overnight funding.

questions.question: What characterises a sell/buy-back compared with a classic repo?
options: It consists of two formally separate trades, collateral income is compensated through the forward price and classically there is no margining
It is always cleared through a CCP
It always has a one-day maturity
It transfers no title to the security
questions.explanation: Sell/buy-backs were traditionally traded without a master agreement and without margining (today often under the GMRA buy/sell-back annex). The coupon is priced into the forward price rather than paid as a manufactured payment.

questions.question: What is an evergreen repo in general market terms?
options: A repo whose maturity rolls forward continuously so a constant notice period remains until it is called
A repo backed only by green bonds
A repo with no interest payment
A repo automatically refinanced with the central bank
questions.explanation: An evergreen with, say, a 95-day residual term keeps its maturity constantly above a regulatory threshold — a popular tool for LCR and NSFR management. On CO:RE this is implemented as the trade-level EVG flag.

questions.question: Why might a buy-side firm prefer a triparty repo over a bilateral one?
options: It outsources collateral selection, valuation and substitution while keeping the credit relationship with the counterparty
Because triparty removes counterparty credit risk
Because triparty repos are exempt from reporting
Because triparty repos never require a haircut
questions.explanation: For a firm without a large collateral operations team, triparty makes secured investing operationally feasible. The credit decision on the counterparty remains entirely its own.

questions.question: Classic repo versus buy/sell-back: where does coupon income on the collateral show up?
options: In a classic repo it is passed back as a manufactured payment; in a buy/sell-back it is priced into the forward repurchase price
In both cases it is retained by the buyer
In both cases it is paid to the triparty agent
In a classic repo it is priced into the forward; in a buy/sell-back it is passed back separately
questions.explanation: The economics are the same, the cash flows are not. This is the practical reason buy/sell-back pricing looks different: income and the funding cost are bundled into one forward price rather than settled separately.

questions.question: How does a market participant typically cover a short position in a bond?
options: Through a reverse repo, to obtain the security needed for delivery
Through a repo in which it delivers the security
By buying an interest rate swap
By placing a deposit with the central bank
questions.explanation: A short seller must deliver, so it sources the paper against cash via a reverse repo. That demand is precisely what turns a bond into a special.

questions.question: Why do banks use repo for liquidity buffer management rather than selling assets?
options: Repo raises cash while retaining the economic exposure and the asset on balance sheet, and is reversible at a known price
Because selling assets is prohibited
Because repo requires no collateral
Because repo removes the asset from the balance sheet
questions.explanation: Repo converts assets into cash without realising a sale, and the fixed repurchase price makes the cost known in advance — the essence of secured funding.

questions.question: What is the main reason a corporate treasury would invest cash via reverse repo rather than a bank deposit?
options: The investment is collateralised, so it reduces unsecured exposure to a single bank
Reverse repos always pay a higher rate
Reverse repos are exempt from taxation
Deposits are not available in CHF
questions.explanation: For large cash balances, deposit concentration risk with one bank is often the binding constraint. Collateralisation is worth accepting a slightly lower yield for.

questions.question: What is a 'matched book' on a repo desk?
options: A book where repos and reverse repos are largely offset, earning the spread and term differences rather than taking directional risk
A book containing only central bank transactions
A book containing only cleared business
A book with no open positions and no revenue
questions.explanation: The matched-book trader is an intermediary: it takes cash from one side and passes it to the other, earning the spread while carrying residual maturity, collateral and liquidity mismatches.

questions.question: How does repo funding relate to a cash-futures basis trade?
options: The cash bond leg is financed in the repo market, so the repo rate is a direct input into the profitability of the trade
Basis trades never involve repo
Repo replaces the futures leg
The repo rate determines the futures delivery date
questions.explanation: If the bond goes special, funding gets cheaper and the basis position becomes more profitable; if repo rates rise, carry can flip negative. This links repo pricing directly to the derivatives market.

questions.question: What does the spread between the GC repo rate and the unsecured overnight rate typically indicate?
options: The market price of counterparty credit risk and collateral scarcity in the money market
The central bank's inflation target
The volatility of the equity market
The cost of settlement in the CSD
questions.explanation: A widening secured/unsecured spread usually signals credit stress or a shortage of high-quality collateral, which is why the relationship is closely watched by central banks.
